ai-at-work.title: Sundar Pichai faces boos, walkout at Stanford graduation ceremony over Google’s Israel, ICE ties
ai-at-work.excerpt: AI is once again at the heart of a college graduation protest — this time for the technology's use in Google's defense contracts.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Google CEO Sundar Pichai got booed and faced a student walkout at Stanford's graduation over the company's defense contracts involving AI, particularly its work with Israel and ICE. This matters to digital workplace professionals because it highlights how employee activism around ethical tech use is becoming impossible to ignore, even at the C-suite level during major public events. Look, when your CEO can't finish a commencement speech without protesters making headlines, your company's got a real internal culture problem that no internal comms campaign is going to fix.

ai-at-work.title: The US government’s Anthropic models ban was never about an AI jailbreak
ai-at-work.excerpt: The Trump administration's decision that forced Anthropic to pull its latest cybersecurity models could be reactionary, retaliatory, or both, but the message is clear: The AI industry isn't immune fro
ai-at-work.dwp_take: The Trump administration pressured Anthropic to withdraw AI security models, citing national security concerns that apparently had nothing to do with actual jailbreaks. This matters because it signals that governments are willing to intervene directly in AI development decisions, which could ripple through enterprise deployments and vendor relationships. Here's the thing: if your workplace tech stack depends on tools that can be yanked by political winds, you're not managing risk, you're just hoping.

ai-at-work.title: Meta’s new ‘AI Mode’ on Facebook pulls from public info across its platforms
ai-at-work.excerpt: Meta announced Monday that it's rolling out a wave of new AI features on Facebook, the latest sign of the company's effort to catch up in the AI race and keep users more engaged on the platform.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Meta is training AI on public data across Facebook, Instagram, and Threads to power new Facebook features aimed at boosting engagement and competing in the AI arms race. This matters to digital workplace pros because it signals how aggressively tech platforms are weaponizing user data and AI to capture attention, which directly impacts how employees interact with company comms on these channels. Honestly, if Meta's answer to "how do we keep people scrolling" is "let's make AI smarter at showing them stuff," we're just automating the engagement hamster wheel at a faster speed.

ai-at-work.title: Cybersecurity vets protest ‘dangerous’ US government ban on Anthropic’s most powerful models
ai-at-work.excerpt: A group made up of dozens of cybersecurity experts urged the White House to remove export-control restrictions on Anthropic’s Fable and Mythos models, arguing that the order is going to limit the abil
ai-at-work.dwp_take: The US government restricted exports of Anthropic's most advanced AI models, and cybersecurity experts are pushing back hard, saying it hamstrings their ability to defend systems effectively. This matters because your IT security team might lose access to tools that actually help them catch vulnerabilities before bad actors do, which is kind of the whole point of having cybersecurity. The irony is thick here: regulators trying to protect us from AI risks may have just made our actual defenses worse, which is what happens when policy gets written by people who don't spend their days actually defending networks.

tools-tech.title: Q&A: A look at forward-deployed engineers, AWS style
tools-tech.excerpt: Hot AI companies can’t stop talking about forward-deployed engineers (FDEs), which are now very much in vogue. FDEs, in case you haven’t heard, are hired by companies looking (hoping?) to successfully
tools-tech.dwp_take: AWS and other hot AI companies are hiring forward-deployed engineers to help customers actually implement AI tools instead of letting them gather digital dust. This matters because it signals that AI deployment is hard enough that companies need specialized staff embedded with customers just to make it work. After thirty years watching software projects fail, I can tell you this is either the smartest staffing move ever or a very expensive way to admit your AI products aren't user-friendly.

tools-tech.title: Why Europe’s demands on Apple AI put your data at risk
tools-tech.excerpt: Europe’s evangelistic approach to insisting Apple open up personal data to competing AI services is hurting Apple users in the region. More than that, it also places its entire business sector at risk
tools-tech.dwp_take: Apple is being forced by European regulators to open up personal data access to competing AI services, which could expose user information to third-party vendors who may not meet Apple's security standards. For digital workplace teams managing employee devices across Europe, this creates a real headache around data governance, compliance risk, and the reliability of AI features that employees depend on daily. Here's the thing: regulators protecting privacy by demanding data sharing is like solving a fire by spraying gasoline, and someone's going to have to clean up that mess in the helpdesk queue.

digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company ran a piece exploring how different personality types respond to different motivational approaches, using a personal finance example to illustrate that fear-based motivation works for some people but actively backfires for others. This matters because most organizations impose one-size-fits-all productivity systems and communication styles that will inevitably demotivate a chunk of your workforce simply because they're wired differently. Here's the truth nobody wants to hear: your company's shiny new engagement initiative probably works great for anxious achievers and absolutely tanks for everyone else, which is why you keep wondering why half your people seem checked out.

digital-culture.title: Xbox plans layoffs, even after Microsoft CEO said company is ‘long on gaming’
digital-culture.excerpt: In July, Xbox may be the next brand hit with major changes to its workforce. According to Bloomberg, people familiar with Xbox’s strategy said that it is “planning major job cuts next month,” although
digital-culture.dwp_take: Microsoft is cutting Xbox jobs and marketing budgets despite CEO Satya Nadella's public statements about the company's commitment to gaming. This matters because it shows how quickly executive messaging can diverge from reality, which erodes employee trust and signals that your leadership's public statements might not reflect actual business decisions. After three decades watching tech layoffs, I've learned that when CEOs say they're "long on" something right before cuts hit that division, what they really mean is they're long on shareholder returns.

digital-culture.title: Your best employees are running a second job right now. It’s called summer
digital-culture.excerpt: Every June, my coaching conversations change. The leaders I work with are still talking about strategy and succession, but underneath, a second operating system is running. One client described her su
digital-culture.dwp_take: Microsoft, Google, and other tech giants are seeing their star performers mentally check out and physically unavailable during summer months as childcare and family obligations pull focus away from work. This matters because digital workplace leaders are finally admitting what everyone already knew: your top talent isn't actually there in June, July, and August, and pretending they are just creates resentment and burnout. The real insight here is that companies built for rigid summer schedules are basically asking their best people to choose between their kids and their careers, which is a losing strategy for everyone.

digital-culture.title: Humans aren’t great at identifying ADHD. But AI is
digital-culture.excerpt: The barriers to getting a formal ADHD diagnosis are many: cost, time, the availability of qualified clinicians, a general lack of awareness. Plus, those with inattentive ADHD—which is believed to be m
digital-culture.dwp_take: AI tools are showing promise at identifying ADHD more accurately and faster than traditional clinical assessment, which matters because the existing diagnostic process is expensive, time-consuming, and filled with gatekeepers. For digital workplace leaders, this is crucial because undiagnosed ADHD directly impacts productivity, collaboration tools adoption, and retention, especially among employees who've been quietly struggling for years. Here's the thing though: an AI that spots ADHD in thirty seconds doesn't solve the actual problem if your company still has meeting schedules that would exhaust a normal person, let alone someone with attention regulation challenges.

industry-news.title: Nintendo Alleged Data Breach: Threat Actor Demands $2M Ransom
industry-news.excerpt: Nintendo faces an alleged data extortion incident involving HR records, internal reports, and potential exposure of third-party vendors. The post Nintendo Alleged Data Breach: Threat Actor Demands $2M
industry-news.dwp_take: A threat actor claims to have breached Nintendo's systems and stolen HR records, internal reports, and vendor information while demanding two million dollars. This matters because it shows that even massive companies with serious security budgets can get hit, and when they do, employee data and supply chain details become leverage. The real kicker is that Nintendo probably won't pay, the attacker probably won't delete anything anyway, and meanwhile hundreds of employees are checking their credit reports tonight.

industry-news.dwp_take: Fox is dropping $22 billion to buy Roku and grab access to nearly 100 million streaming viewers while controlling a major connected TV platform. Watching Fox bet the farm on streaming is like watching someone finally fix the roof after the whole house has been flooded for five years.
